questions.q: What did the 1929 study of babies choosing their own food find?
a: Over time the children chose every food and picked healthier options when ill
The children refused most foods and needed constant encouragement
The children preferred sweets and never selected vegetables
The children ate the same amount regardless of what was offered
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes a six-year study where children self-selected from 34 foods without pressure.

questions.q: Why do grandparents often urge children to eat more?
a: They grew up around shortages and want to protect the young from hunger
They believe extra weight is the best cure for childhood illness
They are trying to compete with what the parents provide
They were taught by doctors to increase a child's portions
questions.why: Lesson 2 says memories of war and famine make them equate food with care.

questions.q: What is the only right way to give children good eating habits?
a: Model the behavior yourself rather than forcing them
Offer rewards for finishing every vegetable on the plate
Remove all snacks from the house until they are older
Explain nutritional science to them from an early age
questions.why: Lesson 1 says children see through rules that parents do not follow themselves.

questions.q: How does the summary distinguish appetite from hunger?
a: Appetite is a desire to eat for comfort, not a need for energy
Appetite is physical, while hunger is entirely psychological
Hunger appears only after several hours without food
Appetite is strongest in the morning, hunger at night
questions.why: Lesson 3 says boredom, sadness and frustration make food an easy substitute.

questions.q: Why does forcing children to eat healthy food usually fail?
a: They notice the hypocrisy and simply refuse the food
They are biologically unable to digest vegetables early on
They forget the instruction within a few hours
They eat more when an adult is watching them closely
questions.why: Lesson 1 says pressure backfires, especially when parents do not eat well themselves.
